searchText: The first sentence is false. Indeed PoS is more complex, a **lot more**. As such, surely has more attack vectors on the consensus protocol than pure PoW. It has a few other drawbacks too: it more than doubled the number of people required to be involved when/how to ship upgrades (at least for the first couple of them that need to touch both execution and consensus layers), it increases a bit the required number of blocks to wait before considering your transaction *safe*, it requires users to run two pieces of software if they want to follow the chain without trusting anyone else, with all the configuration issues and risks that that in itself opens, just to name a few. We would be out of our minds if we would be switching to PoS if it was only as a pure brain masturbation. The fact is that PoS has a couple of huge advantage over PoW, not the least of them being **accountability**. It may be easier in PoS to try to fork a few blocks here and then, but do it often and we **will know** who you are and we will be able to come back and punish you for doing so. > it requires users to run two pieces of software if they want to follow the chain without trusting anyone else to be fair, this is just a technical restriction, there's no reason they can't be integrated longer term Highly doubt it, there's zero plans on doing this now, and with all the efforts put into client diversity, that would be huge drawback I'm skeptical that the benefits of improving client diversity outweigh the benefits of the added deployment complexity reducing the population of full nodes like yes having ~4 configurations is nice to ensure that one broken client can't break finality, but having 25 (I think?) different configurations seems like it's more than what's really necessary Agreed I’m hoping they combine someday in the future 🥺 when eth goes back up just buy 4 mansions and move the dev teams in together. couldn't you have a third application launching those two and managing them, eg docker? :) Still it is much better to have one application Having two nodes running opens up exponentially more failures that could happen. The idea of each node having its own P2P and database, with both of them communicating together through an HTTP API is just terrifying. Would have been much better if beacon chain was actually merged into the Ethereum mainnet we have now, not like with the current design that implies “wiring beacon chain and Ethereum mainnet with an Ethernet cable” Post merge I’ll definitely miss running only one Geth without all that mess I don't think its better to have one monolithic application instead of two simpler oners Both of them are extremely complex. As I said, both of them have their own P2P, databases, and they are different chains after all. right, so they would be even more complex together Also I strongly disagree on monolithic applications being bad in this case. Separated microservices are better only when the software is intended to be run solely by you. If you target end users, keep in mind that they’d prefer to not mess with deployment and instead run one software they’d call “Ethereum”. And I think creating problems and funding a *yet another* dev team to fix them is crazy There will be no dapps we have on ETH yeah, you need to do marketing to get them there if people see it significantly better, maybe it works out? Ethereum’s value is not technology but ecosystem If you want changes, you need to start doing such changes. Complaining doesn't take you anywhere unfortunately. Ok I’ll stop A monolithic node controlling what sub-nodes you are running itself could actually help with diversity by running different clients automatically. The first time you run it, you could effectively have it pick a client for you. You don't even really have to merge any codebases just have it internally run 2 seperate clients *for* the end user. It's not too complicated because your having it run the clients for you and gets them talking to eachother etc. For the end user it's just one single "Ethereum" client and for the technical side it's just a managed set of nodes. (I have no experience running the new ethereum stuff, I just write server software) We’re doing this but not on eth 😅 this is what tools like nicenode can provide. The "just press start" solutions with simple UX/UI happen at a higher level than the deep core dev stuff and that's how it should be IMO - permissionless innovation happening in a decentralized way, dont we all love that 🙂 Don't forget about enterprise users who run server nodes on scale, they deserve good UX too FWIW, a hacky way to do this is just to treat nodes as packages. Binance Celsius Blockfi Nexo coinbase etc all use Fireblocks we're talking about a decent % of ETH lost. Technically possible, for sure. excerpts.content: The first sentence is false. Indeed PoS is more complex, a **lot more**. As such, surely has more attack vectors on the consensus protocol than pure PoW. It has a few other drawbacks too: it more than doubled the number of people required to be involved when/how to ship upgrades (at least for the first couple of them that need to touch both execution and consensus layers), it increases a bit the required number of blocks to wait before considering your transaction *safe*, it requires users to run two pieces of software if they want to follow the chain without trusting anyone else, with all the configuration issues and risks that that in itself opens, just to name a few. We would be out of our minds if we would be switching to PoS if it was only as a pure brain masturbation. The fact is that PoS has a couple of huge advantage over PoW, not the least of them being **accountability**. It may be easier in PoS to try to fork a few blocks here and then, but do it often and we **will know** who you are and we will be able to come back and punish you for doing so.
